title: TOEFL Listening 2026: The Four Task Types
summary: How Listen and Choose a Response, plus conversations, announcements and academic talks work in the new adaptive Listening section.

nodes.label: Choose a Response
nodes.note: Hear a prompt, pick the best reply

nodes.label: Two-stage adaptive
nodes.note: Difficulty shifts after the first stage

chunks.heading: Listen and Choose a Response — functional English
chunks.body: You **hear a short spoken prompt and choose the most appropriate response**. It tests everyday, functional listening — recognising what a natural, polite reply sounds like.
chunks.realExample: You hear: 'Would you mind if I joined your study group?' The best response is something like 'Not at all — we meet on Tuesdays,' not a literal 'Yes, I would mind.'
chunks.memoryHook: Pick the reply a real, polite speaker would give — function over literal words.

chunks.heading: Conversation & Announcement — campus situations
chunks.body: You listen to a **campus-life conversation** and to an **announcement** in an academic or campus setting, then answer questions. Listen for the **purpose** (why are they talking?) and the **key detail or change**.
chunks.realExample: An announcement: 'Tomorrow's lab session is moved from Room 210 to the Science Annexe.' Expect a question on what changed — the new location — so catch specifics like rooms, times and dates.
chunks.memoryHook: Catch purpose + the one detail that changed (room, time, date).

chunks.heading: Academic Talk — the mini-lecture
chunks.body: You hear a **short academic talk** from a professor or expert and answer questions on the **main idea and supporting points**. Take brief notes — you can't replay the audio.
chunks.realExample: A talk on why bees waggle-dance: jot 'main = communicate food location' and one or two supports. Your notes, not your memory, answer the detail questions.
chunks.memoryHook: Note the MAIN idea first, then 2 supports. Notes beat memory.

chunks.heading: It's adaptive — and you can take notes
chunks.body: Listening is **two-stage adaptive**, so the first stage shapes the difficulty of the second. You **can take notes throughout** — build the habit so you're not relying on recall.
chunks.realExample: Use a quick shorthand: arrows for cause/effect, a star for the main point. Consistent note symbols save you seconds you don't have.
chunks.memoryHook: Always be note-taking. First stage sets the level — start sharp.

recall.q: What do you do in the 'Listen and Choose a Response' task?
recall.a: Hear a short spoken prompt and choose the most appropriate, natural response — it tests functional listening.

recall.q: What should you listen for in the conversation and announcement tasks?
recall.a: The purpose of the exchange and the key detail or change, such as a new room, time or date.

recall.q: What is the best strategy for the academic talk task?
recall.a: Take brief notes of the main idea and a couple of supporting points, since you can't replay the audio.

recall.q: Is the Listening section adaptive, and can you take notes?
recall.a: Yes — it's two-stage adaptive, and you can take notes throughout.

recall.q: Why do the early Listening items matter?
recall.a: Because the first stage sets the difficulty of the second stage in the adaptive format.
